What is MongoDB and how does it differ from a relational database?

MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database storing BSON documents in collections with a flexible schema. Relational databases store rows in tables with a fixed schema, normalise data and use joins. MongoDB typically embeds related data in one document, scales horizontally with sharding, and models data around application access patterns, while relational DBs excel at complex joins and strict relational integrity.
When would you choose MongoDB over MySQL, and vice versa?

Choose MongoDB for varying or evolving attributes (product catalogs, CMS, profiles), hierarchical aggregates read as a whole, high write volume, or when horizontal scaling is a priority. Choose MySQL/PostgreSQL for highly relational data, complex ad-hoc reporting with joins, strict constraints and foreign keys, and multi-entity transactions as the norm (finance, billing). Many systems use both (polyglot persistence).
What is BSON and what is an ObjectId?

BSON is a binary encoding of JSON-like documents that is fast to traverse and supports extra types such as Date, ObjectId, Decimal128, 32/64-bit integers and binary data. An ObjectId is a 12-byte default _id: a 4-byte timestamp, a 5-byte random value and a 3-byte counter, so it's unique without coordination and roughly sortable by creation time (getTimestamp()).
Embed or reference – how do you decide?

Embed when data is owned by the parent, read together, and bounded in size (one-to-few) – you get one read and atomic updates. Reference when the related data is large, unbounded, shared among many documents, or updated independently (many-to-many, one-to-many with thousands of children). Hybrid patterns like subset or extended reference embed only the frequently needed part.

What does $unwind do and when is $lookup used?

$unwind deconstructs an array field, outputting one document per element – useful before grouping by array items (e.g. sales per SKU from order line items). $lookup performs a left outer join with another collection in the same database, adding matching documents as an array field; it can also run a sub-pipeline. Heavy reliance on $lookup may indicate the schema should embed more.
What types of indexes does MongoDB support?

Single-field, compound, multikey (arrays), text, geospatial (2dsphere), hashed (sharding), wildcard, plus options like unique, partial, sparse and TTL. A TTL index on a date field deletes documents after expireAfterSeconds via a background task that runs about every 60 seconds – useful for sessions, OTPs and temporary tokens.
How do you design a compound index? What is the ESR rule?

Order fields by Equality (exact matches) first, then Sort fields, then Range filters ($gt, $lt, $in on large sets). For find({status:"PAID", total:{$gt:500}}).sort({createdAt:-1}) the index is {status:1, createdAt:-1, total:1}. The index also serves queries on its leftmost prefix, so avoid redundant indexes.
How do you analyse a slow query?

Run .explain("executionStats") and check whether the winning plan is IXSCAN or COLLSCAN, compare totalDocsExamined to nReturned, and look for in-memory SORT stages. Use the database profiler or slow-query log (and Atlas Performance Advisor) to find slow operations, then add or adjust indexes, add projections and limit result size.
Does MongoDB support transactions?

Yes. Every single-document operation is atomic, including updates of nested arrays. Multi-document ACID transactions are supported on replica sets (4.0+) and sharded clusters (4.2+) with snapshot isolation. They have performance cost and a default 60-second lifetime, so prefer schema designs where a business operation touches one document. In Spring, use @Transactional with a configured MongoTransactionManager.
What is a replica set and how does failover work?

A replica set is a group of mongod nodes holding the same data: one primary for writes and secondaries that replicate the primary's oplog. If the primary becomes unreachable, the remaining members hold an election and promote a secondary, typically within seconds; drivers with retryable writes reconnect automatically. Use an odd number of voting members (e.g. 3) to keep a majority.
What is sharding and how do you pick a shard key?

Sharding distributes a collection's data across multiple shards for horizontal scale, with mongos routing queries using the shard key. A good key has high cardinality, distributes writes evenly, and is included in most queries so they target one shard. Avoid monotonically increasing keys (timestamps, ObjectIds) with ranged sharding because all inserts hit one shard – use a hashed or compound key instead.
What are write concern and read preference?

Write concern sets how many nodes must acknowledge a write: w:1 (primary only) or w:"majority" (default, survives failover), optionally with journaling. Read preference chooses which members serve reads: primary (default, consistent), primaryPreferred, secondary, nearest. Reading from secondaries scales reads but may return stale data. Read concern controls the consistency level (local, majority, snapshot).
MongoRepository vs MongoTemplate?

MongoRepository provides CRUD, paging and derived query methods (findByStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc) plus @Query JSON queries – minimal code for common cases. MongoTemplate gives full control: dynamic Criteria, partial updates with Update ($set, $inc), upserts, findAndModify, bulk operations and aggregations. Many services use both – repositories for basics, a custom repository with the template for complex queries.
How do you implement pagination efficiently?

skip/limit (Spring's Pageable) is simple but gets slower with deep pages because skipped documents are still scanned, and a total count adds another query. For large data sets or infinite scroll use keyset pagination: sort on an indexed unique field and query { _id: { $lt: lastId } } with limit. Spring Data supports this with Window/ScrollPosition.
How do you store money and dates correctly in MongoDB?

Use Decimal128 (Java BigDecimal, mapped with a converter or @Field(targetType = FieldType.DECIMAL128)) for currency to avoid floating-point errors, or store integer minor units (paise/cents). Store timestamps as BSON Date (UTC, Java Instant), not strings, so range queries, sorting and TTL indexes work.
How do you enforce some structure on a schemaless collection?

Use schema validation with $jsonSchema on the collection (required fields, types, enums), with validationLevel and validationAction (error or warn). In the application, rely on typed domain classes (Spring Data @Document), Bean Validation, unique indexes, and a schemaVersion field to migrate documents gradually (tools like Mongock help).
How do you update one element inside an array, or all elements matching a condition?

Use the positional operator $ to update the first element matched by the query ({"items.sku": "A"} then $set: {"items.$.qty": 3}), $[] for all elements, and the filtered positional operator $[name] with arrayFilters for all elements matching a condition. All of these are atomic within the document. In Spring Data, Update.set("items.$[i].status", ...) combined with update.filterArray(Criteria.where("i.status").is("UNPAID")) does the same.
How do you prevent lost updates in MongoDB with Spring Data?

Two complementary techniques. First, avoid read-modify-write: send atomic operators ($inc, $set, $push) with updateFirst or findAndModify, optionally with a condition in the filter (for example stock >= qty) so the update only applies when the rule holds. Second, when you must load and save a whole document, add @Version: the save includes the version in the filter and throws OptimisticLockingFailureException on a conflict, which you retry or report as 409.
@DBRef vs @DocumentReference vs storing the id yourself?

@DBRef stores a {$ref, $id} object; it is resolved with one extra query per reference (N+1) and $lookup handles it awkwardly. @DocumentReference (Spring Data MongoDB 3.3+) stores just the id (or a custom key) and can resolve lazily, which is leaner. Storing a plain id field and loading related data explicitly, or with $lookup in an aggregation, is the most transparent and usually the recommended choice. If you find yourself needing many references per read, revisit the schema: embed or duplicate the fields you read together (the extended reference pattern).
What are change streams and how do you make a consumer survive restarts?

Change streams let an application subscribe to data changes (built on the oplog, so a replica set is required). Each event has a resume token in _id; persist it after you process the event and reopen the stream with resumeAfter or startAfter. Processing should be idempotent because a crash between handling and saving the token replays the event. If the token has fallen off the oplog window, the stream cannot resume and you need a full resync, so size the oplog for your longest expected outage. In Spring, use MongoTemplate with a MessageListenerContainer or ReactiveMongoTemplate.changeStream(...).
How do you test Spring Data MongoDB code?

Use the @DataMongoTest slice, which configures MongoTemplate and repositories only, with a real MongoDB from Testcontainers: @Container @ServiceConnection static MongoDBContainer mongo = new MongoDBContainer("mongo:7");. The Testcontainers MongoDB module starts a single-node replica set, so transactions and change streams also work. Avoid embedded or in-memory fakes: index behaviour, aggregation stages and transactions differ. Create indexes in tests the same way as in production (migration tool or explicit ensureIndex), since auto-index-creation is off by default.
How do you insert or update a million documents efficiently?

Use bulk writes: insertMany or bulkWrite in the shell, BulkOperations in Spring (mongoTemplate.bulkOps(BulkMode.UNORDERED, Order.class)), in batches of a few thousand. Unordered mode lets the server continue after an error and parallelize; ordered stops at the first error. Use upserts (updateOne with upsert: true) for idempotent re-runs. For a one-off load, consider creating secondary indexes after the import, and use write concern majority if the data must survive a failover.
What are read concern and causal consistency?

Read concern controls how durable the data you read is: local (default, may later be rolled back after a failover), majority (acknowledged by a majority, will not roll back), linearizable (most recent majority write, single document, slow), and snapshot inside transactions. Combined with write concern majority, it gives durable reads. Causally consistent sessions guarantee read-your-own-writes and monotonic reads even when reads go to secondaries: the driver passes the operation time of your last write so a secondary waits until it has caught up.
MongoDB or PostgreSQL with jsonb?

PostgreSQL jsonb gives flexible documents with GIN indexes alongside relational tables, joins, constraints and mature transactions, which suits mostly relational data with some variable attributes. MongoDB is stronger when the document is the main model: rich update operators on nested arrays, an aggregation pipeline, built-in horizontal scaling with sharding, change streams, and integrated search in Atlas. Pick by data shape and team skills; many teams avoid running both unless there is a clear reason.
What are time-series collections and when would you use them?

A time-series collection (MongoDB 5.0+) is created with timeField, an optional metaField (for example a device id) and a granularity. MongoDB stores measurements internally in compressed buckets (the bucket pattern done for you), which cuts storage and speeds time-range queries. Use it for metrics, IoT readings, vitals or audit-style events, usually with a TTL via expireAfterSeconds. Updates and deletes are more limited than in normal collections, so it fits append-mostly data.
Can MongoDB do vector search for AI features?

Yes, on Atlas (and in recent self-managed editions): you store embeddings as an array field, define a vector search index, and query with the $vectorSearch aggregation stage to find the nearest neighbours, optionally pre-filtered by metadata. This lets a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) feature keep documents, metadata and embeddings in one store. Spring AI has a MongoDB Atlas vector store integration. Atlas Search ($search) covers full-text relevance search, and both can be combined in hybrid search.
find() vs aggregate() vs mapReduce: which do you use?

| find() | aggregate() | mapReduce
Filter, sort, limit, projection | Yes | Yes ($match, $sort, $limit, $project) | Only a query filter
Group, join, reshape | No | Yes ($group, $lookup, $unwind, $facet) | Yes, with JavaScript functions
Uses indexes | Yes | Yes, for $match / $sort at the start of the pipeline | Only for the query filter
Status | Core API | Core API | Deprecated since MongoDB 5.0
Spring Data | Derived queries, Query + MongoTemplate.find | @Aggregation, Aggregation.newAggregation | Avoid in new code
Aggregation agg = newAggregation(
    match(Criteria.where("status").is("PAID")),
    group("customerId").sum("total").as("spent"),
    sort(Sort.Direction.DESC, "spent"),
    limit(10));
List<CustomerSpend> top = mongoTemplate
    .aggregate(agg, "orders", CustomerSpend.class)
    .getMappedResults();
Rule of thumb: use find() when you return documents as they are stored; use aggregate() as soon as you group, join or compute fields. Rewrite old mapReduce jobs as pipelines.

ObjectId vs UUID vs a natural key for _id?

| ObjectId | UUID | Natural key (e.g. MRN, email)
Size | 12 bytes | 16 bytes (BSON binary) | Varies
Generated by | Driver, no round trip | Application | The business
Order | Roughly increasing (starts with a timestamp) | v4 random; v7 time-ordered | Depends
Index inserts | Append to the right edge: cache friendly | v4 spreads writes over the whole index | Depends
As a shard key | Ranged: all inserts hit the last chunk; use hashed | Spreads well | Depends on distribution
Can change later | No: _id is immutable, so a value the business may correct is a poor _id
Interview tip: ObjectId is the safe default. If you use java.util.UUID, set spring.data.mongodb.uuid-representation=standard so other drivers read the same bytes. Keep natural keys such as a medical record number in a separate field with a unique index.
Replica set vs sharded cluster: what does each one solve?

| Replica set | Sharded cluster
Solves | High availability, read copies, backups | Data size and write throughput beyond one server
Data per node | A full copy | A subset (chunks by shard key)
Writes go to | The single primary | The primary of the shard that owns the key
App connects to | The members (replicaSet in the URI) | mongos routers
Extra parts | None | Config server replica set and mongos
Failover | Election of a new primary | Per shard, because every shard is itself a replica set
Rule of thumb: every production deployment is at least a replica set. Shard only when one primary cannot keep up with the writes or the data set, and choose the shard key first, because most queries should include it.
